verdicts.reason: I could not refute 18.2137 h. It is the strongest family (0.1116; weighted 0.1165) with bootstrap family fractions of 0.98 unweighted and 0.99 weighted. All 3 longitude groups agree. The two leave-one-out subsets that disagree are driven by the TESS-only 1280 h trend, which R1 treats as an artifact. My fold_plot run gives a 2/2 fold with amplitude 0.113 mag. I also checked the ground data alone (2921 points): 18.2137 h has power 0.102 and 5.14753 h has 0.046. Prewhitening one period leaves the other at exactly the same period (5.14753 h at 0.055; 18.2137 h at 0.111). In TESS alone the two are equal (0.117 vs 0.115). Fitting both periods together gives amplitudes of 0.097 and 0.056 mag in the ground data and 0.130 and 0.101 mag in TESS. Both signals are present in every well-sampled apparition, with 18.21 h usually the stronger. 5.1475 h is neither a harmonic nor a daily alias of 18.21 h, and it folds cleanly into two maxima and two minima (amplitude 0.081). So the data contain two real, independent periodicities, which points to a binary or a non-principal-axis rotator. The rules favour 18.2137 h because it is the stronger signal and dominates the bootstrap. However, the data cannot show which periodicity is the rotation of the main body, so quality C is kept, with 5.14753 h as the competing solution. 9.1068 h is the single-wave half of 18.21 h, not an independent alternative. sigma_P = max(9.4e-5, P^2/(2 dT) = 6.76e-4) h.

The 5.3561/2.6781 h family (power 0.412) has bootstrap family fractions of 1.00 in both the unweighted and weighted periodograms. The daily alias at 4.378 h (rotation frequency differs by 1 c/d) reaches only 0.138 and has family fraction 0.00. My fold_plot run (four-term model) shows a clean two-maxima, two-minima light curve at 5.35614 h with amplitude 0.514 mag, so doubling the period is excluded under R2. The 4.378 h fold is weaker (amplitude 0.30, rms 0.246 vs 0.202). The support is independent: 3 of 3 longitude groups and 13 of 13 leave-one-out subsets agree, and Gaia (P07G), which has no daily aliases, picks 2.6781 h. The single datasets that prefer the 4.378 h alias family are single-site sets whose top two peaks are nearly equal (2nd/1st 0.92-1.00). The manuscript P_c = 5.537 h sits on a peak of power 0.015, at the 5-sigma threshold of 0.0144, and folds into noise (amplitude 0.12). The manuscript's separate-dataset period P_av = 5.357 h agrees with 5.3561 h. sigma_P = max(2e-6, P^2/(2 dT) = 7.35e-5) h.

I tried to rescue the primary-range value 45.47 h and could not. (1) Ground data alone (TESS excluded) prefer 895.2/447.6 h (0.186) over 45.47/22.74 h (0.147). The preference survives three tests that would remove a phase-angle systematic. With per-dataset offsets plus a global polynomial in phase angle, or a per-dataset quadratic, the long period stays at 0.186-0.19. With separate offsets for each dataset and apparition it still gives 0.173 vs 0.137. (2) Each apparition analysed separately gives a period near 445-458 h (twice that is about 890-915 h) as its best period, with power 0.39-0.60, beating the best short period every time. In the apparitions observed from several longitudes (South Africa M22o, Chile W68, Tenerife R17w, Gaia P07G), 22.74 h is weak (0.07-0.16), so the daily alias is broken. (3) TESS is an independent test. A long-period model fitted to the ground data only, without TESS, predicts the TESS 24-day brightness trend in phase and sign (correlation +0.80 to +0.85). The ground-only 45.47 h model does not (correlation 0.16). After a cubic detrend, TESS has power 0.005 at 45.47 h. Injecting the ground-fitted 45.47 h light curve into the TESS data would give power 0.19, far above the 99.9th percentile (0.055), so TESS excludes 45.47 h at that epoch. The 45.47 h family is exactly the 1.0019 c/d window alias of the long-period signal. Its family fraction is only 0.70/0.73, so it is not a satisfactory primary-range solution, and the long-period exception in R1 applies. Under R2, 447.6 h folds into a single wave (amplitude 0.34), while 895.2 h folds into two maxima and two minima (amplitude 0.31) with equal power, so 895.2 h is adopted. My 200-sample night-block bootstrap puts 99.5% of resamplings in the 895 h tooth for all data (scatter 0.41 h) and 89% for ground only, where 10.5% fall in the 914 h tooth. The long period beats 45.47/22.74 h in 100% of all-data resamplings and 94.5% of ground-only ones. Therefore sigma_P = P^2/(2 dT) = 2.0 h. Quality stays B, not A: the neighbouring 914 h tooth is not fully excluded in ground data, the Americas group alone still ties at 22.74 h, and the TESS data are quantized.

verdicts.reason: The period of 4.11493 h holds up. I am raising the quality from C to B because the reviewer's claims of 'no TESS support' and 'no subset confirms it' are wrong. My checks were run in scratchpad with exact chi2 Lomb-Scargle. (1) TESS alone, which has no daily aliases: after detrending each visit, the strongest peak in 0.8-240 h is 4.1177 h (power 0.090), with its half 2.061 h second. The 1.0007 h peak disappears (0.006), and 24.04 h (0.018) and the daily alias 3.79 h (0.015) are negligible. Each usable visit peaks on its own at 4.114-4.120 h: 2018 at 4.114/2.057, 2020 at 4.120 and 2023 at 4.117. These visits used different cadences (30 and 20 min), so the peak is not a cadence effect. The TESS folds are double-peaked with minima near phases 0.25 and 0.75, but the data are quantized at 0.1 mag. (2) ZTF I41r alone has its top peaks at 2.0568 and 4.1142 h. (3) Ground data with the per-dataset nightly median removed: the 24.04/48.09 h family vanishes (0.006/0.004), which proves it comes from nightly zero-point offsets and rejects it under R4. The top peaks there are 2.0571 and 4.1142 h. The daily alias 3.789 h is weaker (0.026 vs 0.035), and TESS rules it out. (4) 1.00065 h is a TESS sampling artifact: 2f is about 48 c/d, the 30-min sampling frequency. 1137.8 h comes from TESS trends and is rejected under R1. (5) The double, 8.23 h, has power 0.0076, below the threshold. The 2.057 h fold is single-wave and the 4.115 h fold is double-peaked (2/2), so R2 selects 4.115 h. The quality is B rather than A because the family bootstrap fractions (0.66 u, 0.58 w) are pulled down by the artifact families, the amplitude is only about 0.11-0.16 mag, and the comb tooth is uncertain. The noise-weighted and nightly-demeaned ground data prefer the 4.1142 h tooth, and only 55 % of resamplings stay in one tooth. So sigma_P is the scatter over all teeth, 0.00037 h, which is larger than P^2/(2dT) = 4.1e-5 h. Note for the pipeline: its single-dataset periodograms appear to use fastchi2, which I found returns power > 1 on small subsets (for example 703G gave 1.56 with fastchi2 and 0.42 with exact chi2). That probably explains why every single dataset was reported at exactly 24.044 h.

I could not refute 12.29639 h. The fold at 12.296 h is coherent and double-peaked, with 0.27 mag amplitude and unequal minima (14.53 and 14.60). The fold at 6.148 h, which has equal power, is a single wave, so R2 selects 12.296 h. Its double, 24.59 h, has no power (0.021), so doubling again is excluded. The family bootstrap fraction is 1.00 in both periodograms, and 100 % of resamplings stay in the same tooth. The one real concern was that single datasets and single-longitude groups do not break the 0.5 c/d daily alias. With exact chi2, Hawaii-only data give 0.368 at 16.54 h vs 0.350 at 12.30 h, Chile/Arizona/NM give 0.216 vs 0.159, and several datasets (T05o, T05c, D29R, G45r) prefer 16.54 h. I tested this. Instrument-independent multi-longitude partitions both strongly favour 12.296 h: ATLAS alone (5 sites) gives 0.306 vs 0.181 at 16.54 h and 0.092 at 9.785 h, and non-ATLAS surveys give 0.303 vs 0.099 at 16.54 h and 0.122 at 9.785 h. The 12.296 h power stays high when groups are combined (coherent), while the 16.54 h power collapses to 0.110 (incoherent). The Europe/Africa and Asia/Australia groups each lean to 12.296 h, and the ground data with nightly medians removed also rank the 12.30/6.148 h family first (0.016-0.017 vs 0.009 and 0.006). The manuscript's 9.785 h (power 0.095, bootstrap 0, fold rms 0.160 vs 0.142) and 16.542 h (0.110, rms 0.158) are daily aliases. The solution is not day-commensurate: 2f = 3.904 c/d. sigma_P = max(2.6e-5, P^2/(2dT) = 4.27e-4 h) = 0.00043 h.

verdicts.reason: Survives my checks. The two TESS visits, taken 4 years apart, each find the 7.78/3.89 h pair as their top peaks on their own (visit 1: 7.784 h, power 0.138; visit 2: 7.778 h, 0.073). Neither visit shows power near 24 h (0.02-0.03). A 7.79 h model fitted to the ground data predicts TESS with r=+0.19 (random periods: sd 0.03, maximum 0.10) at scale 1.1. A 24 h model predicts TESS at scale only 0.17, so the 24/48 h comb is a ground-only effect. It is coherent between the Americas and M22o (r=+0.64), which shows that ground systematics are shared across sites, not that the object rotates in 24 h. I subtracted 20-day medians from each dataset to remove slow variations. After that the 24/48/12 h family and 6.70 h drop below 0.008, while 7.787-7.790 h and 3.894 h (0.042) remain the only significant peaks. TESS rejects the k=1 daily alias 6.70 h (0.006), although the ground data rank it slightly above 7.79 h. The 7.79 h fold is double-peaked, so R2 gives 7.79 h rather than 3.895 h. Quality stays C (R5): amplitude is only about 0.08 mag, the combined bootstrap family fraction is 0.04/0.02, and M22o anti-correlates (r=-0.24). On sigma: the bootstrap scatter over all teeth is 0.0013 h, but after the 20-day filtering the 7.7865, 7.7874 and 7.7900 h teeth are almost equally strong, so I keep the more conservative 0.0021 h.

Confirmed. 6.741 h (0.374) folds into a single 0.47 mag wave (1/1), while 13.482 h (0.370) is double-peaked (2/2) with slightly unequal minima. R2 therefore gives 13.482 h, and a 0.47 mag amplitude also requires a double-peaked light curve. The family bootstrap is 1.00/1.00, with 14/14 leave-one-out subsets and 2/2 longitude groups agreeing. My own cross-predictions confirm it. Models fitted to the Americas predict M22o at r=+0.73 (scale 1.1) and P07G+D29R at r=+0.57. Models fitted to Hawaii predict all other stations at r=+0.58. The k=1 daily aliases fail: 10.526 h and 5.263 h give r=-0.72 on M22o, and the manuscript's 18.762 h gives r=-0.19/-0.10/-0.13. The three single datasets that pick an alias (T08o, T05o, 703V) are each at one longitude and cannot break daily aliases. Sigma is P^2/(2dT) = 0.00052 h; the within-tooth scatter is only 2.3e-5 h.

Quality stays C, but 23.979 h is not the more plausible solution. Its bootstrap preference (0.56/0.66) comes entirely from the Hawaii data (T08o/T05o/T05c/T08c/F51w). My night-block bootstrap gives the 24 h family 0.96 on the Hawaii data but only 0.19 on the 418 non-Hawaii points (W68o, M22o, G45r, 703G). On those points the 3.831 h pair (0.26) and its k=1 daily alias 4.163 h (0.32) win together in 0.58 of resamplings. A 24 h model fitted to Hawaii does not predict W68o+M22o (r=-0.05, random periods sd 0.08). The 3.831 and 4.163 h models do (r=+0.16/+0.18), and Americas models at 3.83/4.16 h predict M22o at r=+0.44/+0.45 (random periods sd 0.12). The 24 h fold is phase-clumped and day-commensurate, with no TESS data (R4). After removing slow variations (20-day medians per dataset), 1.915/3.831 h is the strongest family (0.057/0.056), ahead of 2.082/4.163 h (0.048). The day-commensurate 7.987 h falls to 0.011. R2 picks 3.831 h, which is double-peaked (0.12 mag, full phase coverage), over the single-peaked 1.915 h. The alias ambiguity with 4.163 h (double-peaked, 0.12 mag, top in the weighted periodogram) is unresolved, so the quality stays C. The manuscript's 4.56 h (4.5596 h tooth) belongs to the same alias chain: rotation frequencies 6.265, 5.765 and 5.264 c/d are spaced by 0.5 c/d, so 4.56 h is the k=2 daily alias of 3.831 h. Sigma is the scatter over all teeth (only 0.59 of resamplings stay in one tooth) = 0.00039 h, larger than P^2/(2dT) = 0.00007 h.

C and 'period undetermined' are correct, and the evidence is stronger than the reviewer stated. The whole 96/k h comb is the daily alias of a slow brightness variation at the orbital period, not a rotation signal. The comb frequency is f=1.001270 c/d (2f=2.002540). The spectral-window peaks minus 1/P_orb (1380 d) are 1.001278 and 2.002518 c/d, within 2e-5 c/d of the comb (resolution 1.3e-4). A low-frequency periodogram peaks at about 1290-1380 d (power 0.25-0.33). The station-to-station correlations follow the longitude differences, as nightly sampling of a non-rotational variation predicts. At 47.94/23.97 h, T08o predicts M22o at r=-0.66 and W68o at about 0; at 11.98 h, T08o predicts M22o at +0.65 and W68o at -0.50. A genuine rotation would correlate positively at every station. Subtracting 20-day medians per dataset removes the entire comb (47.94 h: 0.003; 15.97 h: 0.007). That filter would also suppress a real day-commensurate signal, so this step alone is not decisive. What is left is only a marginal 1.764/3.528 h pair (0.018/0.015, about 0.05 mag, cross-subset r +0.08 to +0.10). The 15.97 h member (near the manuscript's 15.997/15.976 h) correlates between Hawaii and Chile (r=+0.45) but not with M22o, and it vanishes with the rest of the comb. No alternative is better supported, so the bootstrap-preferred, double-peaked 47.94 h is kept as a nominal value at quality C. Sigma is the scatter over all teeth (0.046 h).

R1 is satisfied. The primary-range comb (236.7, 231.1, 227.1 h, ...) comes from TESS, is single-peaked and fails every independent check (0/2 groups, 0/15 leave-one-out, 0/10 single datasets). The 572/1144 h signal comes from many ground datasets at different longitudes: without TESS, W68o, M22o, 703V, G45r, T05o and R17w each on their own. My cross-predictions give Americas to M22o+R17w+D29R r=+0.74 and ground to TESS r=+0.6 to +0.65 (scale about 0.9-1.0). 46.066 h (manuscript 45.98 h) and 24.98/49.96 h are daily aliases of the long-period harmonic (2f = 1.0027 - 0.042 or 1.0 + 0.042 c/d). On the harmonic: 1144 h is the strongest peak (0.524) and double-peaked (2/2), while 572 h (0.494) is a single 0.47 mag wave in every subset with both 2 and 4 terms. R2 and the large amplitude therefore give 1144 h. The ground data alone give equal power at the two periods (0.412/0.414), so the two halves of the light curve are not shown to differ; the choice rests on fold shape and amplitude. Quality B is appropriate. Sigma is P^2/(2dT) = 3.2 h.

R1 is satisfied. The primary-range peaks are a TESS-driven, single-peaked comb with no independent support. The 633/1266 h signal appears in T08o, T05o, T05c, 703V, P07G, G45r and W68o individually. My cross-predictions give Americas to P07G+M22o+R17w r=+0.65 to +0.72 and ground to TESS r=+0.84 to +0.89, so the signal is real. 46.19 h (manuscript 46.16 h) is weak (0.027) and not confirmed. On the harmonic: 633 h is the strongest peak (0.436), but its fold is essentially a single wave. It is 1/1 in the ground-only 2-term fold, and in the combined fold the second maximum is only about 0.1 mag against about 0.45 mag for the main wave. A single-waved 0.5 mag light curve is physically implausible, and 1266 h (0.390, ratio 0.89, comparable) is double-peaked, so R2 gives 1266.55 h. One caveat: the long TESS visit covers 1510 h (1.2 cycles of 1266 h) and fits 633 h as well as 1266 h (rms 0.0889 vs 0.0915 with 2 terms; 0.0875 vs 0.0870 with 4). The two halves of the 1266 h light curve are therefore nearly identical, not 'clearly unequal' as the reviewer stated. This is still consistent with a normal double-peaked light curve, but 633 h remains the harmonic alternative. Quality B. Sigma is P^2/(2dT) = 4.4 h.

Several ground-based datasets support it (Americas group, W68o Chile, G45r, 703V, and the without-T05o and without-W68o runs), which satisfies the R1 long-period exception. The manuscript's 57.34 h is the daily alias of 2f(291 h) (28.668 h = 1/(1.0021 - 0.1649 c/d)). Sigma = P^2/(2dT) = 0.20 h.

verdicts.reason: I could not refute 547.431 h. It has power 0.358 (weighted 0.353) against 0.130 for the best primary-range peak, and it beats the best primary candidate in 100% of bootstraps. The 26.25, 12.53 and 22.03 h peaks are the 547 h second harmonic (0.0877 c/d) shifted by the 1.0019 and 2.0038 c/d window peaks. The 52.50 h fold is weak (rms 0.249 against 0.2135 at 547.43 h). The 4-term fold at 547.43 h is clean and double-peaked (2/2, amplitude 0.49 mag); 273.71 h is a single wave. So R1 (long-period exception, with Polakis as external support) and R2 both give 547.43 h. My own checks fill the reviewer's gaps. (1) Every ground-based dataset on its own has a strong peak at 530-550 h (power 0.33-0.68), including T08o, T05o, T05c, W68o, M22o, D29R, P07G and R17w, so several longitudes support it. The largest datasets (T08o, T05o, T05c) put it at 547.4-547.6 h. (2) A night-block bootstrap I ran over 500-600 h (200 resamplings) kept the 547.4 h tooth in 100% of cases, with scatter 0.03 h. (3) The neighbouring teeth are weaker than the reviewer stated: power 0.148 at 535.51 h, 0.072 at 531.31 h and only 0.023 at Polakis's 532.9 h. Sigma = P^2/(2dT) = 0.74 h. I keep quality B rather than A because the period is above 240 h and the 2.7% offset from the single-apparition value of Polakis (2020) is attributed to synodic-sidereal drift but has not been shown to be.

Quality C is correct, but 23.973 h is not the more plausible member under R2, which comes before R3. In the 2-term fit at 23.973 h the first harmonic dominates (A1 = 0.083 mag against A2 = 0.055 mag). The 4-term 2/2 count comes from a weak, irregular secondary hump (minima 0.31 apart in phase), so the fold is not clearly double-peaked. The double of that period is present with comparable power: 47.830 h has power 0.158, which is 95% of 0.166. It is labelled 2P in the peak families and is the strongest comb tooth within 0.24% of 2 x 23.973 h; the exact double, 47.946 h, has power 0.125 and folds 3/3. At 47.83 h the second harmonic dominates (A2/A1 = 1.6, with negligible A3 and A4), giving a regular double-peaked curve. Fitting each of the 14 datasets on its own gives the same pattern in 13 of them: the best peak near 24 h is dominated by a single wave (A2/A1 < 1), while the best peak near 48 h is double-peaked (A2/A1 > 1). The separate-dataset manuscript value (47.848 h) agrees. The case for 23.973 h is statistical only: bootstrap 0.73/0.68 against 0.24/0.28 and weighted power 0.136 against 0.104. That is why this is a downgrade to C, not a clear overturn. R4 keeps it at C in any case: both solutions are day-commensurate, there is no TESS data, and the global model explains variance in the Hawaii and Arizona datasets (T05c, T05o, T08o, 703G, G45r, about +0.3 to +0.4) but not in W68o (Chile), M22o (South Africa) or P07G, so the signal lacks cross-longitude support. Sigma: only 62% of resamplings stay in the 47.83 h tooth. My bootstrap over the 48 h comb gives a scatter of 0.055 h over all teeth, which is larger than P^2/(2dT) = 0.006 h.

92.753 h survives. It has power 0.229 (weighted 0.226), its family wins 100% of bootstraps in both periodograms, all 12 leave-one-out runs agree, and the tooth is stable (same tooth 1.00, second tooth 0.54). The 4-term fold is clearly double-peaked (2/2, amplitude 0.33 mag, A2/A1 = 1.6). The half, 46.38 h, is a single sinusoid (A2/A1 = 0.3). The double, 185.5 h, has power 0.059 and an irregular 4/4 fold. The manuscript's 31.589 h is the 1.002 c/d alias of 2f (power 0.080, bootstrap 0). The reviewer worried that longitude coverage is too narrow to break this alias, so I tested it directly. The global 92.75 h model explains variance in every one of the 12 datasets (+0.10 to +0.37), including the non-American M22o (+0.12) and D29R (+0.12). The 31.59 h model makes both worse (M22o -0.49, D29R -0.20), so the South African and Chinese data reject the alias even though their single-dataset periodograms cannot separate the two. The solution is not day-commensurate (2f = 0.52 c/d), so quality A is justified. Sigma = P^2/(2dT) = 0.0235 h, larger than the tooth scatter of 0.0014 h.

291.058 h survives. The 145.53 h peak is a pure single sinusoid: A1 = 0.220 mag, A2 = 0.034 mag, a 0.47 mag single wave. Under R2 that is not an acceptable rotation solution, and the double has equal power (0.363 against 0.366; weighted 0.383 against 0.389) and folds 2/2 with amplitude 0.49 mag. So R2 gives 2P, and no satisfactory double-peaked primary-range solution remains apart from the alias family. The manuscript's 57.34/28.67 h family is the 1.0021 c/d alias of 2f(291 h): power 0.172, bootstrap 0. The reviewer's concern that some subsets favour the alias does not hold up. On their own, M22o (South Africa) prefers 145.50 h to 28.74 h (0.704 against 0.653) and W68o (Chile) prefers 145.52 h to 28.67 h; D29R and P07G peak at 292.8 and 294.7 h. The global 145.5/291 h model explains variance in all non-Hawaii datasets (M22o +0.52, D29R +0.32, P07G +0.29, W68o +0.59). The 57.34 h model makes M22o (-0.83) and D29R (-0.34) worse. Only the Hawaii ATLAS datasets prefer the alias, which is expected from a single longitude. This satisfies the R1 exception for several longitudes with a coherent fold. The 291.06 h tooth is secure: 287.40 h has power 0.157 and 294.8 h has 0.138, and my bootstrap over 280-300 h kept 100% in the 291.04-291.06 h tooth (scatter 0.013 h). Sigma = P^2/(2dT) = 0.20 h. I keep B rather than A because the period is above 240 h and the choice of P or 2P rests on the R2 shape argument: A1 at 291 h is only 0.03 mag, so the data barely distinguish the two halves of the light curve.

At 11.5691 h the fold is a single wave (1/1) of 0.51 mag, which is not credible as a shape-driven light curve. At 23.13818 h the fold is clearly double-peaked (2/2, 0.52 mag) with the same power (0.262 vs 0.267; weighted 0.292), so R2 selects 23.138 h. 447.16 h survives as the most plausible period, but part of the reviewer's rationale is wrong. The bootstrap fractions in the evidence file are an artifact of a bug. In rebootstrap.py each candidate is searched within +/-20/base (0.0016 c/d). The window of 225.93 h (f=0.10623 c/d) contains the stronger 223.61 h peak (f=0.10733). Both windows then return the same maximum, and np.argmax gives the tie to candidate index 0 (225.93 h). That is why 225.93 h shows win_u 0.71 but same_tooth only 0.15, while 223.61 h has same_tooth 0.79 but win_u 0.00. I re-ran 200 night-block resamplings taking the single global maximum over 0.095-0.12 and 0.19-0.23 c/d. The 223.61 h tooth (the 447 h family) wins 0.71 unweighted and 0.65 weighted. The competitors are 225.93 h (0.14/0.20), 227.56 h (0.13/0.13) and 228.91 h (0.02/0.03). The 223.61 h peak is also the strongest in both periodograms, in 15/15 leave-one-out subsets, and in the americas group and the asia_australia band. In the europe group, 447.2 h is about as strong as the best peak (0.39 vs 0.41), and M22o alone picks it. Several ground-based datasets at different longitudes therefore support it; TESS is not involved. I measured harmonic amplitudes at exact periods. At 223.61 h the first harmonic (0.084 mag) dominates the second (0.042), so the fold is a single wave. The n4 secondary maximum is about 0.02 mag, so the fold is not clearly double-peaked. R2 therefore doubles it to 447.16 h, whose power is comparable (0.088 two-term, 0.103 four-term vs 0.106) and whose fold is double-peaked (0.085 mag second harmonic, 0.18-0.20 mag amplitude). Its two halves are identical: the odd harmonics are about 0.01 mag. So the doubling rests on R2, not on direct evidence. The main primary-range competitor is 225.93 h. Its fold is double-peaked (0.046/0.069 mag) because its power comes mostly from a separate 113 h signal. It is backed by no longitude group and no leave-one-out subset, and wins only 0.14/0.20 in the corrected bootstrap. 455.12 h is the double of the single-wave 227.56 h tooth. 223.61 h is the rotation period only if a single-humped curve is accepted. 26.81 h is not supported (power 0.026). Quality stays C: the family fraction is 0.65-0.71, below 0.8, and the cycle count is unresolved. Sigma uses the scatter over all teeth: my bootstrap winners scatter by 1.54 h (weighted 1.61 h) around 224.5 h, doubled to about 3.1 h. That is far above P^2/(2 dT) = 0.34 h. The reviewer's 2.9 h came from the buggy 225.93 h window.

verdicts.reason: The 130.001 h period holds up. The strongest peak, 65.0005 h, folds as a single wave (1/1). Its double, 130.001 h, has comparable power (0.434 vs 0.439; weighted 0.471) and folds cleanly double-peaked with an amplitude of 0.66 mag, so R2 gives 130 h. Its fold rms is 0.2525, against 0.3011 at the 75.868 h mirror alias and 0.3119 at the manuscript's 35.007 h. The alternatives have much less power: 0.198 and 0.142 unweighted, 0.19 and 0.13 weighted. The family's bootstrap fraction is 1.00 in both periodograms, and all 17 leave-one-out subsets agree. I re-ran the bootstrap resolving individual comb teeth: 100 % of resamplings, unweighted and weighted, stay in the 130.001 h tooth (the next tooth, 129.33 h, has power 0.27). The subsets that pick the 37.93/75.87 h mirror alias are ties, not contradictions: europe_africa 0.779 vs 0.780, asia_australia 0.426 vs 0.429, T08o 0.609 vs 0.644, T05o 0.385 vs 0.487. Each covers too narrow a range of longitude to break a daily alias, and combining longitudes suppresses the alias (Americas group 0.425 vs 0.337; all data 0.434 vs 0.198). The manuscript's 35.007 h differs by 0.501 c/d in rotation frequency, which makes it a daily alias; its bootstrap fraction is 0.00. The long-period peaks (361 h and 367 h, power 0.03) never beat the primary candidate. Quality stays B rather than A: only 1 of 3 longitude groups picks this family on its own (the other two tie with the mirror alias), and there are no TESS data. sigma = P^2/(2dT) = 0.0353 h, which is larger than the bootstrap scatter of 0.0012 h.

105.011 h holds up, and the evidence for it over the adjacent tooth at 105.478 h is stronger than the reviewer stated. The '0.73 unweighted bootstrap win' for 105.478 h is a pipeline artefact. In rebootstrap.py each candidate is searched over +/-20/baseline, a window wide enough to contain the neighbouring tooth (0.0010 c/d away). When two candidates' windows find the same maximum, np.argmax gives the win to the first-listed candidate, which here is 105.478 h. That is why 105.478 h shows win 0.68 but same-tooth 0.05, while 105.011 h shows win 0.00. I re-ran the bootstrap over one 103.5-107.5 h window, with no ties possible: the 105.011 h tooth wins 71 % (unweighted) and 80 % (weighted); 105.478 h wins only 6 % and 11 %. The per-dataset preferences in the evidence have the same problem: mpc_redo.py searches +/-3/baseline of each subset, and for the shorter subsets these windows overlap. Measured at each tooth separately, T05o, T05c, 703G, M22o and W68o prefer 105.011 h; 703V, I41r and T08o (the last marginally) prefer 105.478 h. All 9 leave-one-out subsets prefer 105.011 h (unweighted). Full-data power: 105.011 h 0.1295, weighted 0.1369; 105.478 h 0.0987, weighted 0.1132. The fold at 105.011 h is double-peaked (2/2) with an amplitude of 0.20 mag; 52.505 h is single-waved (1/1). The ground data alone give the same result (52.50 and 105.01 h strongest; 2/2 fold, 0.195 mag). TESS alone, which has no daily aliases, also peaks at about 105/52.5 h (power 0.135) within 20-240 h, so the ~105 h family is independently confirmed. The 1416 h peak comes only from TESS (C57G): its fold is made of the quantised, trending TESS tracks. The 1.000 h peak is also a TESS artefact. Both are rejected under R1. The quality stays C for two reasons. First, the comb-tooth fraction is 0.71 unweighted and 0.80 weighted. Second, the 3.043 h of Fekete et al. (2024) from dense photometry is not detected in the survey data (power 0.005-0.02, amplitude about 0.05 mag, below the 0.010 threshold and below random peaks) but cannot be excluded either. sigma: fewer than 90 % of resamplings stay in one tooth, so the all-teeth scatter from the evidence (0.179 h) applies; it exceeds P^2/(2dT) = 0.030 h.

The 36.08 h family is secure, but the exact comb tooth is not, so I lower the quality from A to B. The strongest peak, 18.0397 h, is single-waved (1/1). Its double, 36.0794 h (power 0.209), folds double-peaked with an amplitude of 0.18 mag and an rms of 0.1138. The 146.164 h alternative is weaker: power 0.078, amplitude 0.11 mag, rms 0.1232. The manuscript table's 20.590 h has power 0.053, and both 146.16 h and 20.59 h differ from 36.08 h by 0.50 c/d in rotation frequency (daily aliases); their bootstrap fractions are 0.00. The family's bootstrap fraction is 1.00 in both periodograms, both longitude groups agree, and 12/12 leave-one-out subsets agree. The single Hawaii ATLAS datasets (T08o, T05o, T05c) favour the 73/146 h alias, but all three nearly tie (ratios 0.91-0.99); one site cannot break a daily alias, and Pan-STARRS F51w/F52w, from the same longitude, prefer 18/36 h. The comb tooth is where the checks disagree. Unweighted, 36.0795 h is higher (0.2092 vs 0.2023 at 36.1326 h), wins 63 % of my tooth-resolved bootstrap, and is preferred by 10/12 leave-one-out subsets. Weighted, 36.1325 h is higher (0.2222 vs 0.2141), wins 71 %, and is preferred by 11/12 leave-one-out subsets. Single datasets split 4 vs 6 in favour of 36.13 h, and 36.13 h matches the old figure's 36.133 h. This is exactly the case A excludes (R3: the weighted periodogram disagrees), so the quality is B. The two teeth are 0.15 % apart, 2 sigma with the all-teeth scatter. I keep 36.0794 h, the peak of the primary unweighted periodogram and the unweighted bootstrap winner. sigma = all-teeth bootstrap scatter, 0.026 h (confirmed by my re-run: 0.026 unweighted, 0.024 weighted); it is larger than P^2/(2dT) = 0.004 h.

results.rationale: Family choice: the 42.61/85.22 h harmonic family wins 100% of the 300 night-block bootstrap samples, both unweighted and variance-weighted (f_u = f_w = 1.00). The next families (85.98/42.99 h and 42.20/84.35 h) have about half the power (0.27-0.28) and win in no sample. The weighted periodogram ranks the same family first (42.611 h at 0.541, 85.219 h at 0.533). Both longitude groups pick 42.611 h: Americas over 28.3 yr, and Europe/Africa (2nd/1st ratio 0.90). All 13 leave-one-out subsets pick 42.611 h or 85.221 h. TESS alone, which has no daily aliases, peaks at 42.663 h and 85.432 h (powers 0.83), the same family within TESS's roughly 10 h resolution at 85 h. Single datasets agree 5/9. The disagreeing ones are short-baseline sets that tie at ratio about 1.00 with the 85.98 h alias (W68o, M22o, R17w), plus G45r, which picks 21.31 h (P/4 of the adopted period, inside the family) at ratio 0.88. Neither 42.61 h (2f = 1.126 c/d) nor 85.22 h (2f = 0.563 c/d) is commensurate with the day. The extended-range peaks (263 h, 251 h) have power 0.014 and never beat the primary candidate, so rule 4 does not apply. Harmonic choice: the two members have the same power (0.5433 vs 0.5432) because the two-term model at 85.22 h adds almost nothing at the odd harmonics. The 42.61 h fold (four-term Fourier) is a single wave of 0.27 mag. The 85.22 h fold shows two maxima (11.42 mag) and two minima (11.70 mag) of nearly equal depth, with amplitude 0.28-0.30 mag, which suits an elongated body. Rule 2 therefore adopts the double, 85.22 h. There is also a little independent support: the four-term fit at 85.22 h has a lower rms (0.08576) than the two- or four-term fits at 42.61 h (0.08686 and 0.08679). This suggests the odd harmonics carry a small real signal, so the two halves are not exactly the same. Comb tooth: 85.2211 h is the strongest tooth, and 100% of bootstrap samples stay in it (sigma_tooth = 0.00056 h). The competing teeth are 85.032 h (0.84), 84.921 h (0.80) and 85.337 h (0.68). The Gaussian fit to the peak gives 85.2203 h, consistent with this. Uncertainty: the resolution floor P^2/(2 dT) = 0.0147 h is larger than the bootstrap scatter, so it sets sigma_P. The provisional grade is A: both bootstrap fractions are at least 0.95, all leave-one-out subsets agree, 2/2 longitude groups and TESS agree, and the period is not day-commensurate.
results.paper_note: (249): the 42.61 h and 85.22 h peaks have equal power, and their family wins all bootstrap samples, both longitude groups, all leave-one-out subsets and TESS. 42.61 h folds into a single wave, so its double, 85.2211 +/- 0.015 h (two maxima and two minima, A about 0.29 mag), is adopted. results.concerns: 1. The choice between 85.22 h and 42.61 h rests mainly on the shape rule (test iv). The periodogram powers are identical and the two halves of the 85.22 h fold look nearly the same. The only extra evidence for the double is the small rms improvement from the odd harmonics in the four-term fit, and TESS (3357 points over 29 d) may drive it. An amplitude of about 0.29 mag supports a double-peaked light curve but does not prove it. 2. The comb-tooth choice is less certain than the bootstrap suggests: the second tooth (85.03 h) has 0.84 of the peak power, and the quality code does not cover the tooth. 3. The 85.98 h alias family is separated from the adopted period by a strong window feature near 0.002-0.005 c/d (window power 0.27 at the difference frequency). It is clearly rejected in the full data but is tied in every short single dataset. 4.
